item.title: Listening to Camille Saint-Saëns- The Swan
item.dc:creator: pedro
item.description: At first, The Swan sounds like a very gentle and beautiful piece. I particularly like how a minor note appears in the melody and suddenly changes the feeling of the music. It brings a small sense of...
item.content:encoded:
At first, The Swan sounds like a very gentle and beautiful piece. I particularly like how a minor note appears in the melody and suddenly changes the feeling of the music. It brings a small sense of sadness or fragility to an otherwise peaceful melody. I think this contrast makes the piece more interesting and prevents it from sounding simply sweet.

The cello, performed by Yo-Yo Ma, and the piano, performed by Kathryn Stott, work very closely together to create the image of a swan moving through the water. The long, smooth lines of the cello make it sound almost as if the swan is singing. The piano has a different role, providing the movement and harmonic support underneath the melody. I especially like the moments when the cello moves upwards while the piano moves downwards. This creates a beautiful sense of expansion and movement between the two instruments.

Towards the end, I really like the way the piano becomes more sparkling and active. For me, it creates an image of the swan shining in the sunlight. The piece therefore feels almost like a small musical picture: the cello represents the swan itself, while the piano creates the water, light, and movement around it.

item.title: Listening to Alanis Morissette – You Oughta Know
item.dc:creator: pedro
item.description: I have been listening to this song for thirty years. I knew it was raw. I knew it was angry. But I never stopped to look at who played on it until recently, and that...
item.content:encoded:
I have been listening to this song for thirty years. I knew it was raw. I knew it was angry. But I never stopped to look at who played on it until recently, and that changed everything about how I hear it.

The lyrics are almost confrontational in their specificity. There is no attempt to disguise the target, no softening for the listener’s comfort. That directness is what made the song feel so real in 1995 and still makes it feel real now. You believe her completely. Whether it is autobiographical or not almost doesn’t matter, because it sounds like it costs her something to sing it.

But this time I was listening differently, because I had just discovered that the bass and guitar were recorded by Flea and Dave Navarro. Two musicians I love, playing on a song I already loved, and I had no idea. Flea’s bass is the thing that gives the track its body. It moves constantly, it has that low-end urgency. And Navarro’s guitar sits underneath everything, restrained, almost uncomfortable, which is exactly right for the song.

What it made me think about was how much a player’s identity can come through even when they are in service of someone else’s work. I didn’t know it was Flea. But I felt something in that bass that I couldn’t name. It turns out it was just him, being himself.
